newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan economy grows in summer, but outlook cloudy.
newsitem.headline: Japan economy grows in summer, but outlook cloudy.

text.p: Japan's economy grew marginally in the summer, raising the prospect of continued growth for some time, but sluggish private consumption clouded the outlook for next year.

The government's Economic Planning Agency (EPA) announced on Tuesday that Japan's gross domestic product (GDP) -- a key gauge of the economy's health -- rose a real 0.1 percent in the July-September period from the previous quarter.
This translated into a rise of 0.4 percent on an annualised basis, it said.
The EPA said the growth figures, which were better than what many economists had expected, confirmed that the economy was continuing to recover and was moving towards a self-sustainable level.

Japan's GDP, which measures output of goods and services minus net income from overseas production, had fallen a real 0.7 percent in the April-June period from the previous quarter, or 2.9 percent on an annualised basis.

"We have confirmed that the gradual recovery is continuing. This will become clearer in the October-December period," Economic Planning Agency Vice Minister Shimpei Nukaya told a news conference after the data was released.
"It is possible for us to achieve the government forecast of about 2.5 percent growth (in GDP) this fiscal year," he said.

Growth in the July-September quarter was led by a rise in exports, largely as a result of a weaker yen against the dollar, which somewhat made up for weak private consumption and lower public spending.
Private consumption, the main engine of growth, fell 0.1 percent in the quarter, and public spending dropped two percent.

Economists said the Bank of Japan may have to maintain its low interest rate policy to help stimulate the economy as growth in the second quarter of the fiscal year was not strong enough to allow for any tightening in credit policy.

The central bank has kept the nation's key interest rates at a record low of 0.5 percent since September last year to keep the economy from falling back into a slump following the end of the 1980s "bubble" era of inflated stock and asset prices.

"I think there is going to be extreme pressure on the Bank of Japan to compensate for the tight fiscal stance by having a continued super loose monetary stance," said Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Baring Securities in Tokyo.
The government plans to cut Japan's huge budget deficit by restraining spending on public works which in the past was used as an effective measure to spur growth.
Economists said growth in the next fiscal year depends on how much private consumption will be affected by a planned rise in Japan's consumption tax from three percent to five percent in April.
Economists said people have been spending more money since the summer ahead of the planned rise in the consumption tax.
"Next year, I can't see growth getting much above one percent... It (the data) shows that the domestic economy is a long way away from a self-sustaining recovery," Jerram said.
Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita said on Tuesday that Japanese companies remained cautious about the business outlook, but overall business activities were firm at the moment.
